prompt: Which two statements describe RSTP port states? (Choose two.)
options: A designated role proves that a port has already reached forwarding.
A discarding port learns user-frame source MACs but sends no BPDUs.
A discarding port forwards broadcasts while holding unicast frames.
A forwarding port learns source MACs and forwards eligible user frames.
A learning port can learn source MACs without forwarding user frames.
explanation: A learning port learns source MACs but does not forward user frames. A forwarding port learns MACs and forwards user frames.

whyWrong.0: A designated port can still be discarding while it moves to forwarding.
whyWrong.1: A discarding port does not learn MACs from user frames.
whyWrong.2: A discarding port forwards no user frames, broadcasts included.

prompt: Which two statements about designated ports are correct? (Choose two.)
options: A segment selects the port advertising the best spanning-tree information.
On ordinary point-to-point links, the root bridge's active ports are designated.
The designated port is selected by the lowest local interface name on each switch.
Every non-root switch must have exactly one designated port per VLAN.
Two links to the same neighbor always make one local port a backup port.
explanation: The segment's designated port is the one advertising the best information. The root bridge advertises cost 0, so its ports on point-to-point links are designated.

whyWrong.2: Root information, cost, BID and port ID decide, not the interface name.
whyWrong.3: A switch can have several designated ports or none, since one is chosen per segment.
whyWrong.4: Parallel links usually give root and alternate roles on the far switch, not backup.

prompt: Which command provides a table of root bridge IDs, total root costs, and local root ports across VLANs?
options: show spanning-tree summary
show spanning-tree root
show mac address-table
show interfaces trunk
explanation: show spanning-tree root lists the root ID, root cost and root port for every VLAN in one table.

whyWrong.0: Summary shows the mode and enabled features, not root paths.
whyWrong.2: The MAC table shows learned addresses, not STP roots.
whyWrong.3: Trunk output shows VLAN carriage and trunk state, not roots.

prompt: Why can an Ethernet loop keep circulating broadcasts through ordinary Layer 2 switches?
options: An STP root port forwards user traffic independently of its state.
Ethernet frames have no hop limit that ordinary bridging decrements.
Learning a source MAC requires a switch to retransmit every frame.
The enclosed IP TTL is decremented by each switch to limit the frame’s lifetime.
explanation: Ethernet frames have no hop count, and switches do not decrement an IP TTL. A looped broadcast therefore circulates until STP removes the loop.

whyWrong.0: A discarding port forwards no user traffic, so state matters.
whyWrong.2: Learning a source MAC does not require flooding.
whyWrong.3: Layer 2 switches do not decrement the IP TTL.

prompt: What does Rapid PVST+ maintain for a network carrying several VLANs?
options: One permanent root elected only when the first switch starts.
A root for each IP subnet, selected from the default gateways.
One root for each physical switch, shared by all its VLANs.
A separate spanning-tree instance and elected root for each VLAN.
explanation: Rapid PVST+ runs a separate instance and root election per VLAN. Two VLANs can have different roots and topologies.

whyWrong.0: The root is re-elected when better information arrives.
whyWrong.1: IP gateways have no role in root election.
whyWrong.2: Instances belong to VLANs, not to switches.

prompt: What does this VLAN 10 interface excerpt show about SW3?
options: Gi0/1 is administratively shut, so its cost is ignored by the switch.
Both Gigabit ports forward because both are operational point-to-point links.
Gi0/2 is a backup port because another port uses the alternate role.
Gi0/2 is the current root port, while Gi0/1 is a standby path.
explanation: Root FWD marks the root port, which is forwarding. Altn BLK marks an alternate port, which discards user frames.

whyWrong.0: An alternate blocked port still runs STP and is not shut down.
whyWrong.1: The blocked port does not forward, whatever the link type.
whyWrong.2: Backup and alternate are different roles, and Gi0/2 is the root port.

exhibit.title: SW3# show spanning-tree vlan 10 — interface excerpt
exhibit.text:
Interface           Role Sts Cost      Prio.Nbr Type
Gi0/1               Altn BLK 4         128.25   P2p
Gi0/2               Root FWD 4         128.26   P2p

prompt: What does this excerpt show about SW1?
options: SW1 reaches the root through Gi0/1 with total path cost 8.
SW1 is the root because the output identifies protocol rstp.
SW1 reaches the root through Gi0/1 with total path cost 4.
SW1 is the root because its Gi0/1 interface is forwarding.
explanation: The Root ID differs from SW1's Bridge ID, so SW1 is not the root. The root block shows total path cost 8 through Gi0/1, and the interface cost 4 is only SW1's part of it.

whyWrong.1: The protocol shows the STP variant, not the winner.
whyWrong.2: 4 is the local port cost, not the total to the root.
whyWrong.3: A forwarding root port belongs to a non-root switch.

Gi0/1               Root FWD 4         128.25   P2p

prompt: For VLAN 20, SW-A has BID 32788.0011.2233.aaaa, SW-B has 28692.0011.2233.ffff, and SW-C has 32788.0011.2233.0001. Which bridge is elected root?
options: SW-B, because its priority field is lower than the others.
SW-A, because its MAC is lower than SW-B's MAC address.
SW-C, because its MAC address is the lowest of the three.
SW-C, because its BID is the last one received by peers.
explanation: The lowest priority field wins, and 28692 is lower than 32788. MAC addresses are compared only when priorities tie.

whyWrong.1: SW-A's priority is higher than SW-B's, so its MAC is not compared.
whyWrong.2: A lower MAC cannot beat a lower priority.
whyWrong.3: BPDU arrival order does not decide the root.

prompt: All switches use the default priority 32768. SW2 enters spanning-tree vlan 10 root primary. What priority does VLAN 10 show for SW2?
options: 32778, because the macro changes only a role label.
24576, because the VLAN ID is omitted from Root ID.
28682, from configurable priority 28672 plus VLAN 10.
24586, from configurable priority 24576 plus VLAN 10.
explanation: The primary macro sets the configured priority to 24576 here. The displayed value adds the VLAN ID, so VLAN 10 shows 24586.

whyWrong.0: The macro changes the priority number, not just a label.
whyWrong.1: 24576 is the configured value, and the display adds the VLAN ID.
whyWrong.2: 28672 is the secondary macro value.

prompt: Both candidates advertise the same root. Using the costs given, which interface does SW4 choose as its root port?
options: Fa0/24, because the route uses fewer switch links.
Gi0/1, because received cost 4 plus local cost 4 is 8.
Gi0/1, because its local interface number is lower.
Fa0/24, because its neighbor is the root itself.
explanation: Root port selection adds the received cost to the local port cost. Via Gi0/1 that is 4 + 4 = 8, and the direct Fa0/24 path is 0 + 19 = 19, so Gi0/1 wins.

whyWrong.0: STP compares path cost, not hop count.
whyWrong.2: Interface number is only a late tie-breaker.
whyWrong.3: A direct link does not beat a lower total cost.

exhibit.title: SW4 worksheet — VLAN 10
exhibit.text:
Candidate   Received root cost   Local port cost
Fa0/24      0                    19
Gi0/1       4                    4

prompt: SW1 has two equal-cost links to the root. Gi0/1 hears sender port ID 128.26 and Gi0/2 hears 128.25. Which becomes the root port?
options: Gi0/2, because its received sending-port identifier is lower.
Neither port, because parallel links require an EtherChannel.
Gi0/1, because SW1's lower local interface number decides first.
Both ports, because equal-cost links share the root-port role.
explanation: With root, cost and sender BID tied, the lower sender port ID wins. Gi0/2 hears 128.25, so it is the root port.

whyWrong.1: STP handles parallel links without EtherChannel by making one an alternate.
whyWrong.2: Sender port ID is compared before the local port.
whyWrong.3: A non-root switch has one root port per instance.

prompt: After a replacement switch was installed, an interswitch link runs classic STP behavior. Which change restores the rapid design?
options: Lower the replacement's VLAN priority to reserve the root role.
Force the replacement's uplink to shared link type for safety.
Configure `spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst` on the replacement.
Enable PortFast on both ends of the interswitch transit link.
explanation: The replacement is in PVST mode, which uses classic behavior. Set spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst on it.

whyWrong.0: Priority affects root election, not rapid versus classic mode.
whyWrong.1: A shared link type disables the rapid handshake.
whyWrong.3: PortFast does not fix a mode mismatch on a transit link.

exhibit.title: Replacement SW2# show spanning-tree summary — excerpt

prompt: An engineer sets spanning-tree vlan 30 cost 2 on SW1 Fa0/24. What does it do?
options: The root bridge changes its BID to include 2; every switch repeats that new BID.
The peer changes its receiving port cost to 2; SW1 keeps its own automatic cost.
SW1 raises the physical link speed; neighboring switches learn the new bandwidth.
SW1 uses cost 2 for that candidate; a changed advertised root cost can affect neighbors.
explanation: The command changes SW1's VLAN 30 cost on that port. If SW1's root cost changes, the cost it advertises changes, which can alter neighbors' decisions.

whyWrong.0: Cost is not part of the bridge ID.
whyWrong.1: The command is local to SW1.
whyWrong.2: STP cost does not change link bandwidth.

prompt: The link stays up but an RSTP port misses three BPDUs at a 2-second hello. What does that mean?
options: The bridge must wait exactly 50 seconds before detecting the missing neighbor.
The bridge has proved the fiber transmit strand is physically broken.
The bridge can age the neighbor information after about six seconds.
The bridge guarantees that all application traffic recovers in six seconds.
explanation: Three missed 2-second hellos is about 6 seconds, after which the port ages out the neighbor's information. This does not identify the physical cause.

whyWrong.0: The 50-second figure belongs to classic STP timers.
whyWrong.1: Several faults stop BPDUs while the link stays up.
whyWrong.3: Detecting the neighbor loss is separate from full traffic recovery.

prompt: A new switch has VLAN 10 priority 4096. The root SW1 was set with root primary. What happens with no guards?
options: The new switch wins because its configured priority is lower than 24576.
SW1 retains the role because the macro permanently marks it as primary.
SW1 automatically subtracts 4096 from the newcomer's advertised priority.
The new switch waits for SW1 to fail before it may participate in elections.
explanation: The primary macro just set SW1's priority to 24576. The new switch's 4096 is lower, so it becomes root.

whyWrong.1: Primary is a configuration shortcut, not a permanent status.
whyWrong.2: No process lowers a competitor's priority.
whyWrong.3: A new switch takes part in the election at once.

exhibit.title: SW1 running-config excerpt
exhibit.text:
spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst
spanning-tree vlan 10 priority 24576

prompt: Two ports of one switch connect to the same hub segment. One hears the switch's own BPDUs. What role does that port have?
options: Backup, because it backs up this bridge's attachment to the same segment.
Designated, because each local interface must advertise onto the hub.
Alternate, because every redundant cable provides a path through another bridge.
Root, because a received BPDU always selects the path toward the root.
explanation: A backup port is a redundant attachment to a segment where the same switch already has a designated port. An alternate port reaches the root through a different switch.

whyWrong.1: A segment has one designated port.
whyWrong.2: The BPDU comes from the same switch, not another bridge.
whyWrong.3: Receiving a BPDU does not make a port the root port.

prompt: SW-A and SW-B both advertise root cost 8 on their shared segment. Which end becomes designated?
options: SW-B, because its sending bridge ID is lower at the tied advertised cost.
SW-A, because its port number is lower than SW-B's port number.
SW-A, because its local interface cost of 4 is lower.
SW-B, because designated-port selection prefers the higher link cost.
explanation: Both advertise cost 8, so the lower sender bridge ID decides. SW-B has the lower BID, so SW-B is designated.

whyWrong.1: Sender BID is compared before port number.
whyWrong.2: Local port cost is not a tie-breaker for designated ports.
whyWrong.3: No rule prefers the higher cost.

exhibit.text:
SW-A                  SW-B
Root ID          same                  same
Advertised cost  8                     8
Sender BID       32778.0001.0001.0001   28682.00ff.00ff.00ff
Local port cost  4                     19

exhibit.title: Supplied spanning-tree worksheet
exhibit.text:
SW-A BID: 30.00aa.0000.0001
SW-B BID: 30.0010.ffff.ffff
Both belong to the same connected VLAN 30 instance.

prompt: Both VLAN 30 candidates use priority zero. Which wins?
options: SW-A wins because priority zero prevents any other root claim.
They retain separate roots because both configurable priorities are zero.
SW-A wins because the MAC comparison prefers the higher value.
SW-B wins because its MAC is lower after the priority fields tie.
explanation: Both priority fields are equal at 30, so the lower MAC address wins. SW-B has the lower MAC and becomes root.

whyWrong.0: Priority zero does not stop the MAC tie-breaker.
whyWrong.1: All connected switches agree on one root per VLAN.
whyWrong.2: The lower MAC wins, not the higher.

exhibit.title: Supplied spanning-tree worksheet
exhibit.text:
Same root ID received on both ports.
Gi0/1: advertised cost 4; local cost 4; sender BID 32778.0001.0000.0001; sender port 128.1
Gi0/2: advertised cost 4; local cost 4; sender BID 28682.00ff.0000.0001; sender port 128.48

prompt: The candidates advertise the same root and equal total cost. Which SW-C port becomes the root port?
options: Gi0/1, because the sender port number is lower.
Gi0/2, because the sending bridge ID is lower.
Both, because equal-cost spanning-tree paths are load shared.
Gi0/1, because the local receiving port number is lower.
explanation: Both totals are 8, so the sender BID is compared before any port ID. Gi0/2 hears the lower BID and wins.

whyWrong.0: The sender BID decides before the sender port ID.
whyWrong.2: A non-root switch has one root port, and STP does not load share.
whyWrong.3: The local port is a later tie-breaker and is not reached.

exhibit.title: Supplied spanning-tree worksheet
exhibit.text:
Rapid PVST+; VLANs 10 and 20 present and allowed on all triangle links A-B, A-C, B-C.
All receiving costs are 4 for both VLANs.
VLAN 10 priorities: A 24576, B 28672, C 32768.
VLAN 20 priorities: A 28672, B 24576, C 32768.

prompt: C links only to A and B. Which root port does C use in each VLAN?
options: C-A for both VLANs because the lower VLAN number wins the election.
C-B for both VLANs because B is a root in one instance.
Both physical links in both VLANs because each VLAN needs two root ports.
C-A in VLAN 10 and C-B in VLAN 20, based on the separate instances.
explanation: Each VLAN runs its own election. C uses the direct link to each VLAN's root, so C-A in VLAN 10 and C-B in VLAN 20, and one port can have different roles per VLAN.

whyWrong.0: VLAN numbers do not compete in an election.
whyWrong.1: B is root only in VLAN 20.
whyWrong.2: C has one root port per instance.

exhibit.title: Supplied spanning-tree worksheet
exhibit.text:
Same VLAN 10; both local port costs 4; no guards.
Gi0/1 advertises root BID 32778.0001.0000.0001, advertised cost 0.
Gi0/2 advertises root BID 24586.00ff.0000.0001, advertised cost 100.

prompt: A switch receives two advertisements naming different roots. Which is preferred before path costs are compared?
options: Both identities remain roots because their advertised costs differ.
The advertisement on Gi0/1, because advertised cost zero beats cost 100.
The advertisement on Gi0/1, because the receiving port number is lower.
The advertisement on Gi0/2, because it identifies the lower root BID.
explanation: Root bridge ID is compared before cost. The advertisement naming the lower root BID wins even with a higher cost.

whyWrong.0: A connected instance has only one root.
whyWrong.1: Cost does not override a better root BID.
whyWrong.2: Port number is compared much later.

exhibit.title: Supplied spanning-tree worksheet
exhibit.text:
One VLAN 10; all links bidirectional point-to-point.
Configurable priorities: A 24576; B 28672; C 32768.
A-B cost: 4 at each end.
B-C cost: 4 at each end.
A-C cost: 19 at each end.
No guards, bundles, manual overrides beyond these costs, or other links.

prompt: Which description is correct after this triangle converges?
options: B uses B-C at cost 23; C uses C-A at cost 19; B-A is alternate at B.
B and C both use direct root links; A blocks its higher-cost A-C port.
B uses B-A at cost 4; C uses C-B at cost 8; C-A is alternate at C.
B uses B-A at cost 4; C uses C-A at cost 19; C-B is alternate at C.
explanation: A has the lowest BID and is root. B reaches A at cost 4, and C picks 4 + 4 = 8 through B over 19 direct, so C-A is alternate at C.

whyWrong.0: B has a direct cost-4 path.
whyWrong.1: The root is designated on both links, so the non-root end blocks.
whyWrong.3: C picks the lower cost 8, not the direct cost 19.

exhibit.title: Supplied spanning-tree worksheet
exhibit.text:
One VLAN 10 triangle; no guards or other links.
Original priorities: A 24576; B 28672; C 32768.
A-B: cost 4 at each end; B-C: cost 4 at each end; A-C: cost 19 at each end.
Change: B priority becomes 4096. A and C priorities remain unchanged.

prompt: B alone sets its VLAN 10 priority to 4096. What is the new stable result?
options: A and C each reach B at cost 4; A is designated on the A-C segment.
A reaches B through C at cost 23; C becomes designated on A-C.
A stays root because its previous configured priority was lower than C.
C reaches B through A at cost 23, and A-C is forwarding at both ends.
explanation: B now has the lowest BID. A and C each reach B directly at cost 4, and on A-C A's lower BID wins designated.

whyWrong.1: A also has a direct cost-4 link to B.
whyWrong.2: B's 4096 is lower than A's priority.
whyWrong.3: C has a direct cost-4 link to B.

exhibit.title: Supplied spanning-tree worksheet
exhibit.text:
One VLAN 10, no guards or other links.
Priorities: A 24576; B 28672; C 32768.
Initial symmetric costs: A-B 4; B-C 4; A-C 19.
Only C’s receiving cost on C-A changes to 2; A’s cost on A-C stays 19.

prompt: A is root. C changes only its C-A cost from 19 to 2. Which two results follow? (Choose two.)
options: A loses the root role because C now advertises a smaller cost.
C selects C-A as its root port with total cost 2.
The physical C-A bandwidth increases to match the lower cost.
B becomes alternate on B-C, while C is designated there.
B changes its root path to B-C-A with total cost 6.
explanation: C's direct cost 2 now beats its old cost 8, so C-A is its root port. On B-C, C advertises 2 against B's 4, so C is designated and B's port becomes alternate.

whyWrong.0: A still has the best BID and advertises cost 0.
whyWrong.2: STP cost does not change link bandwidth.

exhibit.title: Supplied spanning-tree worksheet
exhibit.text:
Plan: PC-A and PC-B in VLAN 10, 10.0.10.11/24 and 10.0.10.12/24.
Actual PC addresses/masks match. PC-A connects to SW1 Fa0/5.
SW1 VLAN 10: Gi0/1 Root FWD; Fa0/24 Altn BLK.
All links on the Gi0/1 forwarding path carry VLAN 10 to PC-B.
SW1 show vlan brief: VLAN 20 includes Fa0/5; PC-B port is in VLAN 10.

prompt: PC-A cannot reach PC-B. Which correction fits while keeping the intended tree?
options: Lower SW1’s priority until both interswitch ports have a designated role.
Change PC-B’s mask so frames avoid the blocked SW1 interface.
Reassign PC-A’s port to VLAN 10, then retest through the existing forwarding path.
Disable spanning tree on Fa0/24 so both interswitch paths forward VLAN 10.
explanation: The tree has an active VLAN 10 path, but PC-A's access port is in VLAN 20. Assign it to VLAN 10 and retest.

whyWrong.0: Changing the root does not move PC-A into VLAN 10.
whyWrong.1: The masks match the plan.
whyWrong.3: Forwarding both paths can create a loop and does not fix VLAN membership.

exhibit.title: Supplied spanning-tree worksheet
exhibit.text:
One VLAN 10 triangle before failure: A 24576, B 28672, C 32768.
PC-A is attached only to A; PC-C only to C.
Both PCs are in the same VLAN and subnet. No other devices or links exist.
Failed links: A-B and A-C. Healthy link: B-C.

prompt: Root A loses both uplinks but stays powered. B-C stays up. What happens in VLAN 10?
options: C becomes root of B-C because its priority is numerically greater.
B becomes root of the B-C component, but PC-A is isolated from PC-C.
B becomes root of all three switches, and PC-A uses its default gateway.
A remains the common root and PC-A reaches PC-C through B-C.
explanation: The network splits into two components. B has the lower BID in the B-C part, so B becomes its root, but nothing connects PC-A to PC-C.

whyWrong.0: B's priority is lower than C's, so B wins.
whyWrong.2: One tree cannot span disconnected switches.
whyWrong.3: No path remains from A to the other switches.

prompt: In what increments can you configure the STP bridge priority?
explanation: Priority is configurable from 0 to 61440 in steps of 4096. The default is 32768.

whyWrong.0: Single steps are not allowed, only multiples of 4096.
whyWrong.1: 256 is not a valid step.
whyWrong.3: 8192 is a legal value, but the step is 4096.

prompt: What is the short STP path cost of a 10 Gbps link?
explanation: Short path costs are 100 for 10 Mbps, 19 for 100 Mbps, 4 for 1 Gbps and 2 for 10 Gbps.

whyWrong.0: 1 is not a short-method cost for these speeds.
whyWrong.2: 4 is the cost of a 1 Gbps link.
whyWrong.3: 19 is the cost of a 100 Mbps link.

prompt: What are the default STP hello, max-age and forward-delay timers?
options: 2, 20 and 15 seconds
3, 30 and 20 seconds
1, 10 and 5 seconds
2, 15 and 20 seconds
explanation: The defaults are hello 2, max-age 20 and forward-delay 15 seconds.

whyWrong.1: Those values are not the STP defaults.
whyWrong.2: Those values are not the STP defaults.
whyWrong.3: Max-age is 20 and forward-delay is 15, not the reverse.

prompt: What is the root path cost on the root bridge?
options: The cost of its fastest link
explanation: The root bridge has root path cost 0 and no root port. Every other connected switch picks one root port per instance.

whyWrong.1: The root's cost is 0, not 1.
whyWrong.2: 4 is the cost of a 1 Gbps link, not the root's cost.
whyWrong.3: The root adds no link cost.
